rv.q: The energy expended laughing nearly nonstop for 2 1/2 hours will prove a tonic for any flabby abs.
This new “Spamalot” arrives, beefed up, gussied up and yes, even funnier than in its birthing engagement earlier this year at the Kennedy Center.
The revival has lost none of the smart-dumb charm of either the original musical or its great source of inspiration – the beloved 1975 film Monty Python and the Holy Grail.
This one, directed and choreographed by Josh Rhodes, gives the “ni”-sayers what they want.
There is something liberating for both artists and audiences about a Broadway show that refuses, even for a moment, to take itself seriously.

In the Broadway landscape of 2023, Spamalot turns out to be oddly well positioned to lure people in with the promise of the quotably familiar, then blast them in the face with a confetti cannon full of THEATER (and literal confetti).
Not so with Spamalot, a show that works both as a vessel for Monty Python nostalgia and a platform for the comic talents of this generation of Broadway performers.

This is the showcase role that longtime Kritzer fans—another group that includes, full disclosure, me—have been waiting for, and she grabs it by the throat in a full-tilt comedic and vocal tour de force, culminating in the delightfully ostentatious "Diva's Lament."

Idle’s comic genius remains entirely evident here and he and Du Prez came up with the kind of brassy, swirling score that screamed Big Night Out on Broadway, even as it lampooned everything from scantily clad choruses to divas devolving in Act 2.
Never hilarious, the revival stalls out at pleasant.
But that grail is not to be found here.
The only problem with Spamalot is that it has to end.
It rarely gets any better than this.
The real star of the show is the divine Leslie Rodriguez Kritzer as the Lady of the Lake in what deserves to be a Tony Award-winning turn.
The new iteration of the Monty Python funfest is a welcome dose of both hilarious deconstruction and old-fashioned razzle-dazzle.
Spamalot has no quarter for sadness; it's a fortress of merrymaking that won't let anything serious breach its walls.
Monty Python is timeless, and this Spamalot revival just proves the staying power of its humor.

"Under the guidance of director-choreographer Josh Rhodes, however, this new Spamalot is funny, scrappy, and fast on its feet, thanks to a gaggle of top Broadway clowns, all of whom have apparently been given wide latitude when it comes to ad-libbing.".
Spamalot—the 2005. Tony-winning Best Musical “lovingly ripped off” (as the tagline sayeth) from the 1975 low-budget British movie—is back on Broadway, and it’s as wonderfully silly as ever.
If this production, under the direction of Josh Rhodes, has a fault, it’s that the staging can sometimes be too tongue in cheek for its own good.

Spamalot’s expertly written and performed silliness is endless, beguiling, and winning, and so well-done that—despite the gay and Jewish clunkers of songs—the musical remains a daffy, rollicking night out.
“Spamalot” is high-stepping, low-brow and often hilarious.

Even peppered with choreographic references to an iconic Drag Race lip sync and the sounds of Grindr notifications, Lancelot’s big coming-out disco number is more or less a relic, amusing primarily through the gauze of nostalgia.

But alas, as with many other whose near-two-decade cobwebs were only lightly dusted off, I was left to consume a number about a character’s coming out that, until the final moments when a few Grindr beeps came through, comprised what a 2005 straight man’s idea of gayness was like.
The mustiness now is downright allergy-inducing.
Brilliantly directed by Rhodes, 'Spamalot' is diverting and entertaining.
But as Arthur and his misfit entourage prove, a little comedic muscle goes a long way.
A safe "Spamalot" doesn't lack shelf-life in 2023, but it could be funnier.
Delightful for some, confusing for others.

cn.t: Critics largely embrace this energetic revival as hilariously silly escapism, praising the talented cast and fast-paced direction, though some find the humor dated and question whether the show needed to return so soon.

vs.sum: The St. James Theatre offers good sightlines for most seats, though the lack of a solid rake can be an issue if someone tall sits in front of you. The sound quality is generally good, but the tight legroom can be uncomfortable for taller patrons. The theater's ambiance is enhanced by its historic and grand interior, while facilities are average with standard amenities.

acc.note: No steps from sidewalk to Orchestra. No elevator. Mezzanine up 29 steps, Balcony up 76 steps.

vr.q: I don't know if it's worth top Broadway ticket prices, but it's certainly a fun night out, especially if you never got to see the original production!
Overall, this is still not a show for me. Um, but I did feel like a lot of the character choices and a lot of the improv made it worth going to see again and made it like that much more enjoyable.
I don't find the material itself to be worth your average Broadway ticket price. the laughs were cheap, and the music sounded cheap.
